title: The Paradox of Memory: Why Forgetting Makes Learning Possible
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick pairs Borges' story 'Funes the Memorious' with Robert and Elizabeth Bjork's research to argue that forgetting is not a flaw in memory but the condition that makes learning and abstraction possible. Funes, who remembers everything, cannot think, because without pruning nothing can be compared, generalised or made meaningful. Hendrick then sets out the Bjorks' new theory of disuse, distinguishing retrieval strength from storage strength and showing why effortful retrieval after some forgetting builds both. From this he derives the case for desirable difficulties such as spacing, interleaving and varied practice, and for treating tests as learning events rather than mere measurement. He contrasts fluent but fleeting methods like rereading and highlighting with spaced, effortful recall, using the crammer versus the spaced learner as illustration. The piece closes by framing forgetting as an adaptive filter, including retrieval-induced forgetting, that lets the mind extract principles and apply knowledge flexibly.
points: Borges' Funes serves as a parable that perfect recall destroys thought, since comparison and abstraction require letting specific details fade.
The Bjorks' distinction between retrieval strength and storage strength explains why a fact can feel forgotten yet remain deeply encoded, and why struggling to retrieve it strengthens both.
Rereading and highlighting create an illusion of learning by boosting momentary fluency, whereas spaced, low-stakes retrieval builds durable storage strength.
Testing is reframed as a learning event in its own right, with feedback closing the loop on failed retrieval attempts.
Forgetting is presented as adaptive, operating across timescales and through retrieval-induced forgetting to keep knowledge current and enable generalisation.
quotes: In Borges' short story Funes the Memorious, the protagonist is cursed with a perfect memory: every leaf on a tree, every fleeting sensation, every trivial detail is preserved. But this gift renders him incapable of thought. With nothing forgotten, nothing can be abstracted, compared, or made meaningful.

A fact can feel inaccessible in the moment (low retrieval strength) but still be deeply encoded (high storage strength). Crucially, each successful act of effortful retrieval increases both. That is why the temporary forgetting we experience between practice sessions actually enhances learning.
In contrast, testing yourself on that same material, even if you fail at first, creates the conditions for storage strength to grow. Effort, not ease, is the signal of long-term learning.

The irony is that the methods that produce the most immediate fluency such as re-reading, highlighting, immediate review, often create the illusion of learning without building lasting retention. Students feel confident because information is readily accessible in working memory, but this accessibility is temporary. The moment the external cues disappear, so does the knowledge.

The Bjorks’ work reveals that forgetting isn't a failure of the memory system, it's an adaptive feature. Our brains are constantly making decisions about what deserves long-term storage. Information that gets repeatedly retrieved and used is marked as important and strengthened.

Perhaps most importantly, this adaptive forgetting creates the conditions for abstraction and generalisation. By allowing specific details to fade while preserving general patterns, our memory system enables us to extract principles, recognise similarities across different contexts, and apply knowledge flexibly.
Far from being the enemy of memory, forgetting then is what makes memory possible. If we remembered everything equally, nothing would stand out. Memory works by filtering, not stockpiling.
